articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket.
articles.title: Authorities arrested a man with ammo and apparently monitoring security at Trump golf course near LA

articles.author: John Ruwitch
articles.description: On their first earnings call since SpaceX's June public offering, executives said the company is pouring funds into rocket development, Starlink satellites and AI.
articles.title: SpaceX's revenue rises as its once-soaring stock price drifts back to Earth

articles.author: Laura Kwerel
articles.description: After Annabelle Gurwitch was diagnosed with stage 4 lung cancer, a volunteer with the same diagnosis encouraged her to stop worrying so much about the future and start living again.
articles.title: A volunteer's unexpected advice changed how she faced cancer

articles.author: Jason Breslow
articles.description: The committee said it was reviewing allegations that Miller "may have engaged in domestic violence." Miller has denied the allegations, which have swirled around his bid for a third term in Congress.
articles.title: House Ethics Committee will investigate Ohio Republican Max Miller

articles.author: Aarti Shahani
articles.description: The fifth and final season of the HBO Max series Hacks is nominated for 24 Emmys, including one for Smart as best actress in a comedy series. The writers "raised the bar every single season," Smart says.
articles.title: 'It's just so fun to make people laugh,' says 'Hacks' star Jean Smart

articles.author: Greg Myre
articles.description: The U.S. and its partners depend on Patriot interceptors to shoot down incoming ballistic missiles. But Russia and Iran are firing their weapons at rates far higher than Patriots can be produced.
articles.title: The soaring demand for Patriot missiles, from the Middle East to Ukraine

articles.author: Scott Horsley
articles.description: A report from Senate Democrats accuses big banks of failing to report suspicious money transfers made by Jeffrey Epstein until after his arrest in 2019.
articles.title: Senate Democrats say banks turned blind eye to suspicious moves by Jeffrey Epstein

articles.author: Robbie Griffiths
articles.description: Europe's heat wave exposes buried history and new threats — Nazi-era wrecks emerge from the Danube, nuclear reactors face cooling risks, and Greece battles deadly wildfires.
articles.title: Europe's heat wave fuels drought, wildfires and fears about energy supplies

articles.author: Maureen Corrigan
articles.description: Daniel Mason's new novel is a spin on Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, in which academics collide with locals — and a few seductive fairies — in the woods of Vermont.
articles.title: 'Country People' is a silly, satisfying midsummer romp

articles.author: Colin Dwyer
articles.description: This month brings riveting novels about dogs, Hollywood stars, small towns and characters with bigger woes than just the sweltering summer heat and humidity.
articles.title: 13 new books in August will get you through the dog days of summer

articles.author: Nick Visser
articles.description:
Follow today’s news live

Alan Jones trial: live updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Almost every house sold in first six months of the year made a profit
The vast majority of homeowners are selling their properties for more than they bought them for, even as house prices enter a tailspin, AAP reports.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Australia news live: ASX hits record high, with investors bullish on peace; brother of former premier Dominic Perrottet appears before Icac inquiry

articles.author: Josh Butler and Benita Kolovos
articles.description:
Exclusive: Warren Pickering told 2025 podcast mass deportations ‘not a reality’ in Australia and suggested politicians over 55 should ‘handball it to the next generation’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One Nation’s Victorian leader has previously said mass deportations in Australia are “not a reality” and “won’t happen”, in newly unearthed comments which raise further questions about Pauline Hanson’s signature policy to deport 75,000 people she says have overstayed visas.
Warren Pickering, on Monday unveiled as the party’s leader for Victoria’s November state election, also previously conceded in niche podcast interviews that the party ran so-called “ghost candidates” who didn’t actively campaign in order to harvest more Senate votes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Won’t happen’: One Nation Victoria leader’s comments raise questions about Hanson’s mass deportations policy

articles.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
articles.description:
Anti-corruption watchdog’s long-awaited report finds ‘serious and concerning’ conduct by senior government members in dealings with union boss

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Senior members of the former Daniel Andrews government engaged in “serious and concerning” conduct in their dealings with the firefighters’ union boss, Peter Marshall, a long-awaited report by the Victoria’s anti-corruption watchdog has found.
The report by the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission was tabled in parliament on Wednesday, some eight years after their investigation first began.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Daniel Andrews’ government engaged in ‘concerning’ conduct but no evidence of firefighter union blackmail: Ibac report

articles.author: Tom McIlroy Political editor
articles.description:
As home affairs minister’s National Press Club address is postponed, refugee advocates lament missed ‘opportunity to bring Australians together’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Labor will introduce new rules to cut net overseas migration and push temporary residents to leave Australia, despite a major speech on the subject by the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, being delayed.
But government sources told Guardian Australia the policy changes would not push net overseas migration lower than the existing targets.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labor plans migration cuts as Tony Burke pulls out of major speech

articles.author: Natasha May in Bangkok
articles.description:
WTA event win earns 21-year-old a presidential reception in the Philippines as interest in tennis surges in home country
The Philippines has been swept up in tennis fever after 21-year-old rising star Alex Eala delivered a historic win, drawing praise from the president who hosted a reception in her honour.
On Monday, Eala became the first player from the Philippines to win a Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) Tour-level singles title.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Our new champion’: Philippines swept up in tennis fever after Alex Eala’s historic win

articles.author: Chris Stein
articles.description:
Wesley Bell wins in St Louis rematch dominated by Israel-Palestine issue
US politics live – latest updates
The Democratic congressman Wesley Bell won his primary in the St Louis area on Tuesday, ending the progressive former representative Cori Bush’s bid for a comeback and blunting the momentum pro-Palestinian candidates have shown in recent elections.
Bell unseated Bush, a democratic socialist who opposes aid to the US ally and accuses it of committing a genocide in Gaza, in the Democratic congressional primary two years ago with the help of millions of dollars in spending from pro-Israel groups. Their rematch this year came amid a spate of primary defeats of Democratic incumbents at the hands of progressive outsiders.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wesley Bell wins Missouri House primary as Cori Bush comeback bid fails

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Jeanine John Taele allegedly took photos and videos of property days before president’s visit
Los Angeles county sheriff’s deputies arrested an armed California man over the weekend who was seen surveilling Donald Trump’s golf course in Rancho Palos Verdes, days before the president was set to arrive there for an event with the Republican National Committee (RNC).
Plainclothes federal agents reported Jeanine John Taele, 38, as a “suspicious individual”, after they observed him on Sunday taking photographs and videos of the golf grounds, located in a coastal town south of Los Angeles, according to county officials.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Armed man arrested at Trump’s California golf course

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Missouri’s top election official has rejected a petition for a referendum on new congressional districts 
Missouri’s top election official has rejected a citizens’ petition seeking a statewide referendum on the state’s redistricting plan backed by Donald Trump.
Supporters of the referendum had submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures in an effort to force a November election on whether to use a new US House map approved by the Republican-led state legislature. But the Republican secretary of state, Denny Hoskins, asserted on Tuesday that the petition was void because congressional redistricting plans cannot be subject to voter referendums.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Missouri rejects citizens’ bid for vote on Trump-backed redistricting plan

articles.author: David Smith Washington bureau chief
articles.description:
Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The US state department said Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti’s visa had been cancelled in retaliation for Brazil’s refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília and its decision last month to deny visas to two US diplomats seeking to visit ahead of an October election.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US revokes Brazil ambassador’s visa in escalation of diplomatic feud

articles.author: Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent
articles.description:
Assessment of more than 2,000 native species warns nearly one in five at high risk of deadly H5N1, including parrots, fur seals and quolls

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

Almost 400 native Australian bird and mammal species have been assessed as being at a high risk – or worse – from the deadly H5N1 bird flu virus, a federal government assessment has revealed.
Some of Australia’s most beloved animals – including species of penguins, fur seals, quolls, dolphins, more than 300 birds and the Tasmanian devil – are considered at least high risk from the virus, meaning they could suffer “severe reduction in population size or viability” or worse if it reached them.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Six additional states caught up in investigation after Michigan reported first two US deaths linked to disease
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the scope of the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states.
The alleged expansion includes the addition of six states, according to the Washington Post, which cited three people familiar with the matter. Those states were Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina, according to a fourth person familiar with the matter who spoke to the paper.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: CDC reportedly expands scope of US cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states

articles.author: Abené Clayton
articles.description:
Trump loyalist, who also has president’s endorsement, has spent millions trying to prove 2020 election was ‘stolen’
Mike Lindell is leaving his role with the MyPillow company to focus on his campaign to become the next governor of Minnesota. In a social media post published on Tuesday, Lindell said that the company was strong enough to withstand his departure.
“This decision is not about walking away. It is about stepping forward to serve. I am putting Minnesota above myself, my title, and my business interests so I can give this campaign and the people of our state my full time, energy, and attention,” Lindell said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mike Lindell, MyPillow CEO, steps down from post to run for Minnesota governor

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Dogs Trust points to hundreds of incidents over recent years, some involving deaths of pets or people
With its gentle rippling water, tall purple flowers and rustling trees, Earlswood Lakes near Solihull in the West Midlands seems the perfect spot for dogs to paddle. But their owners have been warned that the otherwise idyllic open water could prove perilous to pets.
“We’ve had all this hot weather and millions of families are now spending time around open bodies of water, and it’s easy to not realise the dangers,” said Emma-Jane Thomas, rehoming manager at Dogs Trust Kenilworth during a walk around Earlswood.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Campaign warns of perils UK waters can pose for dogs and owners

articles.author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint   made by Labour MP about the funds
An official investigation has been launched into charities in England and Wales donating funds to illegal Israeli settlements in Palestine.
The Charity Commission will aim to establish the amount of charitable funds going to illegal settlements, whether the spending was in furtherance of their purposes and any regulatory action that may be necessary.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Charity Commission to investigate donations to illegal Israeli settlements

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
MI6 has been ranked as the most powerful foreign intelligence service in Europe ahead of France and the Netherlands, according to a peer review.
The British intelligence agency scored 251 points in the research and was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants and penetrating the ruling elites in Russia, China, Iran and Turkey, according to the review by 60 professionals from 25 countries.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review finds

articles.author: Lucy Campbell (now); Nadeem Badshah, Tom Ambrose and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait

Iran and Oman have made progress toward a deal to reopen the strait of Hormuz, a potential breakthrough that could help end the war in the Middle East, regional officials have said.
Under the emerging agreement, ships would enter the Persian Gulf through an Iranian-controlled route and exit through a route controlled by Oman, with service fees charged for providing security and preserving the maritime environment, two regional officials told the Associated Press.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Rubio hopes US can reach Hormuz deal with Iran ‘very shortly’ as officials say progress has been made – as it happened

articles.author: Alexandra Topping Political correspondent
articles.description:
Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Ministers will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.
As part of a government push to reduce the number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Government contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rules

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Masoud Pezeshkian dismisses talk of internal rift as hardline Assembly of Experts call US negotiations ‘futile’

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been forced to deny claims that he has repeatedly threatened to resign as he battles hardline factions opposed to reaching a settlement with the US over the strait of Hormuz.
The US and Europe hope a deal is imminent to reopen the strait and they are putting pressure on Oman to accept a temporary agreement that officials in Muscat fear will leave Iran retaining near permanent dominance of the vital oil shipping channel. Ships would enter the strait in a route close to Iran, but leave on a route that passes through Iranian and Omani waters.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iran’s president denies threatening to resign during talks over strait of Hormuz

articles.author: Penelope MacRae in Delhi
articles.description:
Opposition parties say nationwide protests that forced resignation of education secretary are beginning to dent BJP support
India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata party has lost a byelection in a seat it had held for three decades, after the Cockroach movement student protests that have shaken Narendra Modi’s government.
Prashant Kishor, a high-profile electoral strategist turned politician, scored a breakthrough win for his fledgling Jan Suraaj (Good Governance) party in the Bankipur constituency in Patna, the capital of the eastern state of Bihar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s ruling BJP loses byelection in stronghold after Cockroach student protests

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
articles.description:
Meg O’Neill says ‘where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue’, as company’s profits more than double

Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis

Nils Pratley: BP boss is unsentimental in pruning portfolio and clear on North Sea advice to Burnham



BP’s chief executive has urged Andy Burnham to make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even as the oil company prepares to sell its North Sea business after 60 years in the ageing basin.
In a conversation with the new prime minister, Meg O’Neill said the country should prioritise using energy produced in the UK, “where we generate jobs, we generate tax revenue, we generate all those additional positive impacts”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: BP boss urges Burnham to prioritise UK oil and gas even as firm exits North Sea

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after large air and sea rescue operation by France and UK
A dinghy carrying 173 people has capsized after its engine caught fire as it attempted to cross the Channel from France.
The people onboard were rescued from the water after a large air and sea operation was launched using UK border security and French vessels along with an RNLI boat.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire

articles.author: Agence France-Presse in San Juan Alotenango
articles.description:
Eruption of the Fuego volcano sends lava and ash nearly four miles into the sky as country declares second-highest alert
Hundreds of people living on the slopes of Guatemala’s Fuego volcano have evacuated their homes after a huge eruption spewed lava and plumes of ash.
Central America’s most active volcano erupted on Monday morning, with conditions intensifying by nightfall and prompting authorities to issue the country’s second-most severe alert warning.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Guatemala volcano eruption prompts evacuation of hundreds of people

articles.author: William Christou
articles.description:
Remains of 112 victims, including 40 children, recovered from rubble more than two years after residential block was destroyed
Mourners gathered in central Gaza on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, including 40 children, who were killed in 2023 in one of the deadliest Israeli strikes of the Gaza war.
Their bodies could not be recovered until now because of Israel’s continuing strikes, which have slowed, though not halted, since the ceasefire in October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Mass funeral held in Gaza for victims of 2023 Israeli strike

articles.author: Julian Borger and Patrick Wintour
articles.description:
Optimism echoes Trump’s claims on Monday that deal is close as mediators say they are exchanging proposals 

Middle East crisis live – latest updates

US and Qatari officials have said progress is being made in restoring a ceasefire in the US-Iran war and reopening the strait of Hormuz.
The optimistic speculation on Tuesday brought oil prices down 2%, but the strait remained closed to shipping and a cargo vessel was reportedly struck by an unidentified projectile off Oman’s coast close to the strait.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US and Qatar report progress on Iran ceasefire and reopening Hormuz strait

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Migration commissioner says scheme regularising undocumented people ‘not a good signal’ for Europe

Explainer: Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?

The EU’s top official on migration has criticised Spain’s plan to regularise undocumented migrants as “not a good signal” for Europe, after an emergency meeting intended to draw a line under divisions on the Ceuta crisis.
Magnus Brunner, the European commissioner for migration, said that while the EU could not currently see a direct link between events in Ceuta and Spain’s regularisation plan, the policy was “definitely not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meeting

articles.author: Agence France-Presse in Rome
articles.description:
Winner called waste management team after she realised stub showing she had hit the jackpot had been thrown away
A €1m lottery ticket has been recovered from the rubbish in Italy after the frantic winner called on refuse collectors to help her retrieve it, according to the waste management company.
The instant win ticket was “miraculously still in one piece” after garbage workers combed through mounds of rubbish on their truck, said Roberto Nicola Toscano, the administrator of the SANB company in Italy’s southern Puglia region.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Refuse collectors help Italian woman recover binned €1m lottery ticket

articles.author: Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
Minister tells reporters least 75 people died after EU ministers meet to discuss response to the crisis
Meanwhile, the European Commission said it was “monitoring very closely” the situation in Bulgaria, Hungary and Romania as the region faces an energy crunch caused by the ongoing heatwave and drought.
Energy spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said “the low Danube levels will clearly have an impact on nuclear generation along the route,” and this “concerns several member states.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Spain says 70,000 out of 72,000 migrants that entered Ceuta in mass border crossing have returned to Morocco – as it happened

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Exclusive: More than 60 accounts on X have been made unavailable in Saudi Arabia, after similar action on Snapchat and Facebook
Elon Musk’s X has become the latest major US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi Arabian dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.
Earlier this year, the Guardian reported that platforms including Snapchat and Meta’s Facebook and Instagram had blocked dissidents’ accounts over allegations by Saudi authorities that they were violating local law.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Elon Musk’s X latest to block Saudi dissident accounts inside kingdom

articles.author: Agence France-Press in Geneva
articles.description:
Special rapporteurs say ‘transnational repression by Indian authorities’ has put Moninder Singh in danger
UN rights experts have urged Canada to take all feasible measures to protect the Sikh activist Moninder Singh, who has been repeatedly warned by the Canadian authorities of credible threats to his life.
In a letter to the Canadian government, the five UN experts raised “concerning allegations of foreign intimidation and reprisals” against Singh, a Canadian national.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UN experts urge Canada to protect Sikh activist amid credible threats to his life

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Luis Carlos Rúa revealed himself to be Elefante blanco just three days before election for ‘his own safety’. Now he is tackling graft from senate floor
When 102 senators were sworn in for Colombia’s latest parliamentary session, they included 32 women, 69 men – and one cartoon elephant.
He had some difficulty making his way down the narrow central aisle of Congress’s ceremonial chamber, weaving past fellow senators in sharply tailored suits and dresses, before taking the oath in his pot-bellied white plush costume.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: White elephant in the room: Colombia swears in costumed anti-corruption activist as senator

articles.author: Karen McVeigh and Ayça Aldatmaz in Adana
articles.description:
A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
• ‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problem
High levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub in Turkey supplied with plastic waste by British companies.
The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Most of the zoo’s 16 lions have struggled to cope with high humidity this summer
Three lions from a Tokyo zoo have died from suspected heatstroke and others are undergoing treatment, a spokesperson said on Tuesday, as the big cats struggle in Japan’s high levels of humidity.
Japan sweltered through its hottest summer on record last year and parts of the country have hit 40C in recent weeks, qualifying for the new “cruelly hot day” designation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three lions die of suspected heatstroke at Tokyo zoo as Japan swelters

articles.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
articles.description:
Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour
A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed in New Zealand, ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations.
The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host of kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Prime minister Sanae Takaichi visited Kumamoto prefecture almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 quake hit, killing 38 people
Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has visited the south-western prefecture of Kumamoto, where recovery efforts are being hampered by heat and a lack of water supplies, almost a week after a magnitude 7.1 earthquake killed dozens and caused widespread damage.
Thirty-eight people died during the quake, including one person who died of apparent heatstroke while taking shelter in a car in hot weather, officials said on Monday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan’s prime minister tours earthquake-hit sites as recovery efforts hampered by soaring temperatures

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.
In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Houghwith Ashifa Kassam; produced by Annie La Vespaand Bryony Moore; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin
articles.description:
Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The incident has led to a political crisis in Spain and criticism from EU countries.
Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam – watch on YouTube
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The Latest

articles.author: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid, Okba Mohammad in Ceuta and Lisa O’Carroll in London
articles.description:
Juan Jesús Vivas says influx seen as ‘at least encouraged or permitted’ by Rabat, as Spain demands EU solidarity

Explainer: why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint?

A growing chorus of voices has accused Morocco of helping to fuel the crisis in Ceuta, with the leader of the Spanish enclave describing last week’s border crossings as an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity that was seen as being “if not orchestrated, at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco”.
Spanish officials ⁠said on Monday that an estimated 69,500 people who had arrived late last week in Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa, had returned to Morocco in recent days. About 2,500 people who had made the crossing were believed to still be in Ceuta.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing

articles.author: Natasha May in Bangkok
articles.description:
Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021
Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi has met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed.
The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years of questions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old, whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive

articles.author: Associated Press in Wellington
articles.description:
Pacific nation is latest country to signal a shift away from its colonial past with return to its traditional name
The Pacific Island country of Nauru has changed its name to the Republic of Naoero, its president said, matching the spelling and pronunciation in the national language.
The country’s international code will change from NRU to NRO and its people will be known as dei-Naoero instead of Nauruan. Commonly known abroad by the pronunciation of Now-roo, the new name is spoken as Now-ero.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nauru officially changes its name to Naoero

articles.author: Ed Walton for MetDesk
articles.description:
Soaring temperatures continue to sweep parts of Europe, while Okinawa faces powerful winds and storm surges

Europe live – latest updates

Unbearable, record-breaking heat has dominated the summer of 2026 across much of Europe. New records were set in central Europe last week, with Wieselburg in Austria registering a new July peak of 40.3C (104.5F). This is particularly significant as it is just 0.2C behind the all-time high, set in the August of 2003.
However, not all of the northern hemisphere has experienced extreme heat and aridity. Vancouver recorded its wettest July since 2016 and the third wettest since 2008, with 33.6mm of rain. While that total may not appear exceptional, it is only a touch above the 1991-2020 climate average, highlighting how unusually dry July has been in the Canadian city over the past decade.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Weather tracker: Austria breaks heat records as Japan braces for Typhoon Dolphin

articles.author: Okba Mohammad and Javier Jennings Mozo in Ceuta
articles.description:
People among the more than 50,000 who entered Spanish enclave this week describe the journey and their prospects
Four days ago, Youssef El Abbas saw an opportunity to reclaim the life he had lost seven years earlier. News was circulating that about 400 people had swum from Morocco to the neighbouring Spanish enclave of Ceuta on the north African coast, approximately 12 miles (19km) across the strait of Gibraltar from mainland Spain.
Here was a chance for the 44-year-old Moroccan father of four to return to Spain, from which he had been deported when his residency expired after the loss of his job in Bilbao in 2019.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Chaos of border crossing gives way to limbo for Moroccans on Ceuta’s streets

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Activists in the region say politicians regard LGBTQ+ people as ‘the easiest scapegoats to maintain their power’
A growing number of west African countries are implementing or strengthening anti-LGBTQ+ laws, amid local political pressures and a global pushback against LGBTQ+ rights.
In March, Senegal doubled the maximum prison sentence for gay sex to 10 years and criminalised the “promotion” of homosexuality. Niger criminalised “sexual relations with a person of the same sex” in February, the first time same-sex intimacy had been outlawed in the country.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anti-LGBTQ+ laws are on the rise across west Africa, campaigners warn

articles.author: Dan Collyns in Lima
articles.description:
Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authorities
Police in Peru report that 13 people, among them foreign tourists, have been killed in a plane crash in southern Peru, near the Nazca Lines.
Local authorities in Nazca confirmed that 11 tourists and two pilots died when the Cessna Grand Caravan crashed in Pueblo Viejo, approximately 4 miles (6km) from the city of Nazca and roughly 12km from the Nazca Lines site.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Other members of expedition led by world-renowned climber on Broad Peak also died, climbing company says

Supporters of the referendum had submitted hundreds of thousands of petition signatures in an effort to force a November election on whether to use a new US House map approved by the Republican-led state legislature. Move is retaliation for Lula’s government refusal to approve Trump’s nominee for ambassador in Brasília
Donald Trump’s administration has revoked the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to the US in a sharp escalation of a diplomatic feud with the country’s president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Six additional states caught up in investigation after Michigan reported first two US deaths linked to disease
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reportedly expanded the scope of the largest known cyclosporiasis outbreak to 15 states.
The alleged expansion includes the addition of six states, according to the Washington Post, which cited three people familiar with the matter. Those states were Arkansas, Iowa, Missouri, Nebraska, New Hampshire and North Carolina, according to a fourth person familiar with the matter who spoke to the paper.

articles.description:
Ohioans of Indian heritage will see one of their own take center stage in the race for governor, but their support amid a rocky campaign is not guaranteed
At the Hindu temple of Dayton in south-west Ohio, there’s no little pride for gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy – he and his parents have been coming here to pray for decades.
On a quiet recent Tuesday afternoon, a priest lights incense sticks at the altar of the temple. Outside, a group of first-time visitors take a relaxed walk around the grounds.

articles.author: Arwa Mahdawi
articles.description:
The vocal vaccine sceptic and wife of Trump’s deputy chief of staff turned to the former US science adviser when she was worried about Covid. Now, she’s claiming it was a cunning plan
You should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy and Muslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics to start a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich?
While I may not need to inform you that the Millers are bad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, was forced to appear at a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration.

articles.title: Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite | Arwa Mahdawi

articles.description:
Democrats are pissed off – and they're taking their anger straight to the ballot box. In the wake of Donald Trump's return to the White House, progressives (including members of DSA – Democratic Socialists of America) have defeated established moderates in elections in liberal cities like New York, Washington DC and Seattle. Now, they're trying to win a series of major primaries in the deep-purple midwest. Host Carter Sherman speaks with Guardian midwest political correspondent Rachel Leingang, who has traveled all over the region covering several key races – including this week's Democratic Senate primary in Michigan, where progressive Abdul Al-Sayed is squaring off against the establishment candidate, Haley Stevens. Can leftist politics win outside of blue bubbles? And what do these races reveal about the fight for the midterms and the White House?

articles.title: Mamdani won New York. Can a progressive win the Michigan primary? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

The Greeks learn at Troy that breaking the rules works, then carry the lesson home. Nolan’s film shows how an exception becomes a habit of power

I had not read The Odyssey since I was a student. Stories change when we return to them later in life, or perhaps we are the ones who change. Christopher Nolan’s film made me want to find out what I had missed.
More specifically, it made me want to read Emily Wilson’s translation. Her scathing essay about the film nearly stopped me from buying her translation. I bought the book anyway.

articles.title: Nolan’s Odyssey shows what happens when a leader’s violations are rewarded | Jamil Smith

articles.author: Victoria Bekiempis

After the justice department botched file rollout under the original act, lawmakers now want legislation with teeth 
As Jeffrey Epstein survivors and their supporters continue searching for justice and transparency in the US, a bipartisan group of politicians is trying to rework legislation that heralded the release of long-hidden investigative files on the scandal.

articles.description:
Voters face a choice of progressive ex-congresswoman Cori Bush or pro-Israel incumbent Wesley Bell on Tuesday
The pastor of a historically Black church on St Louis’s north side, Rodrick Burton, has watched with bewilderment as the congressional race in his district has drawn national attention not about the bloodshed in his community, but rather in Gaza.

articles.author: Jan-Werner Müller
articles.description:
The president’s methods, from ‘flooding the zone’ with scandals to prioritizing loyalty over competence, could ultimately weaken rather than strengthen him
The pattern is by now all too familiar: with every power grab Trump tries – from a fraudulent speech about voter fraud to appeals to his supreme court to let him rig the midterms – a debate kicks off about whether these moves are signs of strength or of desperation. Maybe we keep getting caught in this debate because the question is badly posed. So much of what is distinctive about Trump’s governance during his second term can serve the consolidation of an autocratic regime and at the same time create particular vulnerabilities for the regime. We have to become better at identifying these weaknesses, as opposed to being shellshocked by Trump’s brazenness every single time.
Aspiring autocrats operate differently in the 21st century; in previous eras, they had little hesitation about unleashing violence and committing massive human rights violations. Today, they try to fool both domestic and international audiences into thinking that democracy and the rule of law still exist. The recently deposed Hungarian prime minister, Viktor Orbán, was a master of this technique; he spent many years performing what he called “the peacock dance” to convince the European Commission (and Chancellor Angela Merkel) that he wasn’t creating a kleptocratic autocracy.
Jan-Werner Müller is a Guardian US columnist and a professor of politics at Princeton University
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Are Trump’s most blatant authoritarian moves backfiring? | Jan-Werner Müller

articles.author: Andrew Roth and Sufian Taha in Turmus Ayya, West Bank. Photography by Quique Kierszenbaum
articles.description:
After visits by US ambassador Mike Huckabee to the nearby Israeli settlement of Shilo, Palestinian Americans in Turmus Ayya have witnessed a terrifying rise in attacks
No man’s land in Turmus Ayya lies where the US flags end and the Israeli flags begin. It is a few hundred metres of soil scorched by molotov cocktails where Israeli settlers have placed a boulder to tell the Palestinian villagers: this is our land now.
On one side of that boulder are the white-stoned mansions where the Palestinian residents of Turmus Ayya live. About 80% of them are US citizens, members of the diaspora in New York, Chicago and Paterson, New Jersey, who return for the summers and bring their children here to experience Palestinian culture and learn Arabic. Many call themselves proud American patriots and fly the stars and stripes from their balconies.
 Continue reading...

articles.author: Timothy Garton Ash
articles.description:
American democrats need a Hungarian-style landslide to overwhelm Trump’s attempts to rig November’s midterm elections
In these days of extreme weather events, it seems odd to say that the US needs a big landslide. But a landslide defeat for President Donald Trump in November’s midterm elections is exactly what is required if the country is to start reversing his deliberate and rapid erosion of its democracy.
The respected Varieties of Democracy (V-Dem) Institute at Gothenburg University argues that in 2025 the US saw one of the most rapid declines in liberal democracy on record. “Democracy in the USA,” says its Democracy Report 2026, “is now at its worst in 60 years.” As the imperial republic marks the 250th anniversary of its founding, the danger seen at the very beginning of its constitutional order by anti-federalists such as Patrick Henry – that of an overmighty president abusing his executive power in an attempt to become a new king – has come closer than ever before.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Democrats have one last chance to halt the erosion of US democracy – and it’s less than 100 days away | Timothy Garton Ash

articles.author: Hosted by Carter Sherman , produced by Meg Driscoll, engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Jonathan Menjivar
articles.description:
With Republicans' chances in the midterms looking shaky, Donald Trump is increasingly trying to rewrite the rules that govern US elections. Voting rights groups say he's really laying the groundwork to suppress voters. Trump has already moved to change mail-in voting, but he now wants Congress to pass the Save America Act, which includes strict voter ID restrictions. He's also accused China of interfering in the 2020 election. (Trump didn't back up that claim with evidence.) Host Kai Wright speaks with Garrett Epps, legal affairs editor at Washington Monthly, about the threat to US elections and what voters can do to protect them.

Read Garrett Epps' story in Washington Monthly

Donald Trump has declared a breakthrough in negotiations over the disarmament of Hamas in Gaza and the withdrawal of Israeli forces, but IsraelI government officials have voiced scepticism over the deal.

Lucy Hough speaks to Julian Borger, the Guardian’s senior international correspondent
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Can Trump’s Hamas disarmament plan work and will Israel agree to withdraw from Gaza? - The Latest

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman , with David Smith and Rachel Leingang . Produced by Suzanne Gaber and Tiara Chiaramonte , edited by Anabel Bacon , engineered by Ivan Kuraev
articles.description:
Earlier this year, Congress reached a depressing milestone: 86% of Americans, a record high, disapproved of its job performance. But this summer, there have been some signs that shifts are underway. On the left, House Democrats have just voted in unprecedented numbers to withhold military aid from Israel, and across the country, progressive candidates are running competitive primary campaigns that are energizing a base fed up with the status quo. On the right, Republicans are reeling from the sudden death of Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina senator and one of Donald Trump's staunchest supporters. Mitch McConnell, the former Senate majority leader, remains sequestered following a health scare in June, raising questions of if a changing of the guard might be underway there, too. Kai Wright and Carter Sherman are joined by David Smith, the Guardian's Washington bureau chief and Rachel Leingang, midwest political correspondent, to discuss gerontocracy, transparency, the rise of the Democratic Socialists of America and just how much of an inflection point this summer might be for both parties


This page was amended on 23 July 2026. A previous version misspelled Lindsey Graham.

articles.title: Is US Congress finally on the verge of a change? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Official action by regulator for England and Wales comes after formal complaint   made by Labour MP about the funds

articles.description:
UK’s Secret Intelligence Service praised for playing long game and having ‘a taste for dirty tricks’
MI6 has been ranked as the most powerful foreign intelligence service in Europe ahead of France and the Netherlands, according to a peer review.
The British intelligence agency scored 251 points in the research and was commended for its expertise in recruiting high-level informants and penetrating the ruling elites in Russia, China, Iran and Turkey, according to the review by 60 professionals from 25 countries.

articles.title: MI6 is top European foreign intelligence service, peer review finds

Louise Haigh says taxpayer money must benefit local communities amid backlash from environmental groups
Ministers will scrap the requirement for companies to prove their green and progressive values before they are awarded government contracts, and instead ask firms to prove they will help young people back into work.
As part of a government push to reduce the number of people not in education, employment or training (Neets) in the UK and boost regional growth, public sector buyers will double the consideration they give to whether companies will get more people into jobs, rather than if they can show they are improving social and environmental wellbeing. Government procurement contracts account for about £90bn of taxpayers’ money spent each year.

articles.title: Government contracts to require job creation instead of green targets under new rules

Revealed: major oil firms make $93bn profits amid war and climate crisis

All passengers thought to have been taken to Boulogne after large air and sea rescue operation by France and UK

articles.title: Calls to ban disposable barbecues in England and Wales over wildfire risk

The electronic tagging system that will be relied upon to monitor thousands of offenders released early from prison is failing to alert the authorities of potential breaches of conditions, a watchdog has warned.
Martin Jones, HM inspector of probation in England and Wales, said the system relied on hard-pressed police and probation officers looking up individual cases and then deciding whether potential breaches needed to be investigated further.

articles.title: Electronic tagging system failing to alert authorities of probation breaches, watchdog warns

Survey finds party members see health, the economy, cost of living and climate crisis among biggest challenges
Andy Burnham has inherited a Labour membership that is sceptical about increased welfare spending, supportive of higher defence spending, and ranks the climate crisis as one of the country’s biggest challenges, according to new polling.
The survey of 788 members between the end of June and the end of July shows them ranking health (43%), the economy (42%), cost of living (39%) and climate change (29%) as Britain’s most important issues, ahead of welfare benefits (7%) and immigration (6%).
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Labour members ‘have tougher view on welfare than you might think’, poll suggests

articles.description:
Partner of woman killed by dangerous driver among those who say they are devastated at killers leaving jail early

Now, under plans to release prisoners early to ease overcrowding, Adil Iqbal, who filmed himself speeding at 123mph before he crashed into 38-year-old Frankie Jules-Hough, may serve less time in prison than he would have under his original sentence.
“He could actually serve less time than he originally was going to before we appealed,” Buckley said. “We’ve fought for a tougher sentence. What is the point of having an actual sentence if the government can just reduce that?”

articles.title: ‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release scheme

articles.author: Guardian Staff
articles.description:
John Barstow says oil expansion is a necessity, while David Parker wonders if the prime minister will protect the planet or the fossil fuel industry
North Sea oil expansion is a necessity (Burnham risks first revolt as PM over apparent support for North Sea drilling, 31 July). I state this as an environmentalist – not despite. Oil is a feedstock, not mere fuel. Oil is necessary for the day-to-day maintenance of wind turbines, nuclear plants and rail. Hence oil is part and parcel of supply chains for green tech. A domestic oil base brings such supply chains closer. This also underscores the case for approval of coking coal extraction in Cumbria. Green tech needs high-grade steel and high-grade steel needs coking coal.
There are much better ways of helping the environment, such as more tree planting and stopping plastic waste being dumped into our seas. The carbon sink factor would be helped. A major expansion of the UK’s North Sea oil sector will make a more cohesive UK, complete with more jobs in Scotland and the north of England, including in supply manufacturing chains.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: North Sea oil is a litmus test for Burnham | Letters

Poetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poem

UK poetry sales are on course to reach a record high this year, buoyed by the success of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey.

articles.title: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey gives UK poetry sales an epic boost

Rhys Ifans, Matthew Rhys, Aimee-Ffion Edwards and Mark Lewis Jones among actors voicing characters from 1977 blockbuster

But until now, speakers of Welsh – Cymraeg – have not been able to hear the words of Luke Skywalker, Han Solo and Princess Leia spoken in their own language.

articles.title: Star Wars dubbed into Welsh for first time for S4C broadcast

Conservative leader tells press she stands by decision to select Joshua Bonehill-Paine as a candidate for local election in Somerset

Former neo-Nazi activist selected as Tory candidate for Somerset council election

articles.author: Mark Fisher
articles.description:
Beginning his career as an actor, Gill went on to write plays including The York Realist as well as directing for the Royal Court and National Theatre
Tributes have been paid to the director and playwright Peter Gill who died on Monday at the age of 86. His agent Mel Kenyon said Gill’s work had a “rare emotional delicacy” and was “beautifully observed and finely tuned” while the director Michael Grandage said Gill’s “contribution to the British theatre will come to be regarded as quietly seismic”.
Gill began his career as an actor at London’s Royal Court in 1958 when still in his teens. Over the next six years, he played Silvius opposite Vanessa Redgrave as Rosalind in Michael Elliott’s lauded RSC production of As You Like It, as well as several roles in the British premiere of Brecht’s The Caucasian Chalk Circle.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Peter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86

articles.description:
Justice secretary says he could not have gone further without causing system to ‘break’ but acknowledges impact on grieving relatives such as those of PC Andrew Harper
About 1,000 fewer prisoners will be released early after Andy Burnham’s intervention to exclude those convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming from the scheme.
The justice secretary, Alex Norris, said 5,000 prisoners would be released over 10 months from October in England and Wales, down from the government’s original plan for 6,000 from September.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: About 1,000 fewer prisoners to get early release as Burnham tightens rules

articles.author: Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent
articles.description:
£2.2bn project will allow about 100,000 more flights a year to use Britain’s second busiest airport
Gatwick airport is to start development of its second runway after campaigners lost a legal challenge to the plans.
The court of appeal on Tuesday dismissed a bid by local campaign groups to challenge an earlier high court ruling that the scheme could proceed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Gatwick airport to open second runway after legal challenge fails

articles.author: Jessica Elgot Deputy political editor
articles.description:
After a blitz of small wins, PM is finding that like Keir Starmer there is only so much he can control on the big calls
If Andy Burnham wanted to demonstrate he was the anti-Keir Starmer, the first fortnight could not have gone better. Instead of painting a gloomy picture of tough times and an economic black hole that would only improve with sacrifices such as cutting winter fuel allowance, Burnham’s first week was a blitz of small wins including cutting bus fares.
But the new prime minister can only control so much. And like Starmer, within his first days in office he found himself facing immediate decisions where every call will make you unpopular. And – like Starmer – blaming your predecessor counts for nothing with an angry public.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Prisoner early release scheme gives Burnham his first taste of unpopularity

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler and Amee Joshi
articles.description:
This evening service from London to Crewe is hot, sweaty and heaving with people, many having to stand or sit in the gangways
The 5.46pm train from London Euston to Crewe is the low point of Nikhil Patel’s week. “I’ve never gotten a seat. I always stand up even when I get here early,” says the 22-year-old, struggling to keep his balance while the gangway underneath sways from side to side.
Painfully for Patel, who is commuting back and forth to the capital for a computer science internship, it’s the first leg of a three-hour journey home to Walsall. He grabs the back of a chair to remain steady but says he’s just thankful that the train has left on time – and that it’s even on the move at all.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A rail nightmare: what it’s like on England’s busiest commuter-only train

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff Banking correspondent
articles.description:
Levy could raise £19bn to help pay for Andy Burnham’s support for those struggling with bills, say campaigners
Campaigners have renewed calls for a windfall tax on UK banks that could raise £19bn towards Andy Burnham’s cost of living agenda, after HSBC raked in $10.1bn (£7.5bn) worth of profits in the second quarter of the year.
Bosses at HSBC reported on Tuesday that profits rose 60% year on year in the three months to the end of June, helped by fees from wealth management and insurance business, as well as higher interest rates, which allow the bank to charge more for loans and mortgages.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Calls for UK bank tax to fund cost of living help as HSBC profits hit £7.5bn

articles.author: Karen McVeigh and Ayça Aldatmaz in Adana
articles.description:
A Guardian investigation finds irrigation canals polluted with microplastics in Turkey, a major destination for UK waste
• ‘Nobody cares’: Turkish farmers bear the burden of UK’s plastic waste problem
High levels of microplastics and other plastic contamination have been discovered in a waterway close to a major recycling hub in Turkey supplied with plastic waste by British companies.
The polluted waterway, which floods into agricultural fields after heavy rain, feeds into a larger canal used for irrigating crops on the Çukurova plain, in the city of Adana, in the south of the country. It is one of the largest and most fertile agricultural basins in Turkey.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK plastic ‘waste colonialism’ found to be polluting Turkey’s farming heartland

articles.description:
Madeleine Finlay travels to the Rothbury estate in Northumberland, in north-east England. It’s a piece of land that has been in the same family for 700 years, but now it has been put up for sale and the UK’s Wildlife Trusts are trying to raise £30m to secure it intact. To find out what makes the area so special, Madeleine speaks to Katy Barke, the head of nature recovery for Northumberland Wildlife Trust. She also hears from Sam Turner, a professor of archaeology at Newcastle University, who is trying to work out how the land has been used across the centuries. This work will inform the strategy for nature recovery on the site. And Rosie Pearce, a farm liaison officer, explains how the project could bring more wildlife-friendly farming practices to the estate

Northumberland nature recovery project takes shape with biggest land sale in 30 years
 Continue reading...

articles.author: Shane Hickey
articles.description:

Nigel Farage says he would use the military in the Channel but there are questions about whether the plan would work
The Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, whose summer has been dominated by the Guardian’s disclosure of a £5m undeclared gift and his connections with a fraudster, emerged on Monday to claim that his party would launch the “largest military operation in the English Channel since world war two” to prevent small boat crossings.

Several councils to stop housing tenants in glass-fronted Britannia Point in London, where tenants were earlier told they could not use air con

A freeloading tanuki, mounting debt, and a town full of possibilities will sound familiar to fans of Animal Crossing. Alas, while you won’t find accountability from Tom Nook, Kyoto-based studio Denkiworks has stepped in to heal your financial trauma with a BMX-filled adventure in which a mammal finally pays the price for their years of bad behaviour. “Even Japanese people ask why it’s a tanuki,” jokes Liam Edwards, a game designer at Denkiworks. “They have such a mythological background to them; they’re almost like dragons in terms of their mythology.”
In Tanuki: Pon’s Summer, you play as an adorable but irresponsible critter named Pon, who’s bled the coffers of the local shrine – his home – dry by buying video games and snack food instead of preparing for its semicentennial matsuri. As a result, the shrine is in total disrepair, and important architecture and cultural artefacts – such as the ema stand and the chōzuya – are left cracked and broken, unbefitting a festival half a century in the making.

They’re perfect for time-poor cooks, but which deserves your counter space? From combi models to smart designs, here’s what our expert recommends
• The best air fryers 
If you’re at a restaurant and hear a ping a couple of minutes before your meal arrives at your table, it’s unlikely to be a good sign. But microwave ovens are a brilliant tool in the home kitchen. They’re fearsomely fast at heating up – or even cooking – food when you’re time-poor and lacking the energy to make something wholesome after a hard day at work. And in hot weather, cooking by microwave isn’t just quick: it also won’t warm your home.
Microwaves work best for heating food with a high water content (they make the water molecules in food vibrate to create heat). However, before testing, I asked around to find out what people use theirs for most, with a view to using this information to shape my tests. I learned a few things – like lots of people eat mug cakes. Who knew? And that wheat bags are a popular alternative to hot-water bottles. But the majority of folk use their microwave for reheating cold cuppas, defrosting frozen batch-cooked meals, warming food, popping microwave popcorn – and, of course, cooking jacket potatoes more quickly. I used these insights to shape my testing.

articles.title: The best microwaves in the UK for every kitchen and budget – tested

articles.author: Lewis Gordon
articles.description:

The creators of Untitled Goose Game return with an online, open-world adventure that delivers slapstick silliness and bucolic majesty in nearly equal measure
Radiant sunsets glinting on lapping waves; bushland valleys that beckon with secrets; modernist buildings sat atop craggy ridges: Big Walk’s setting is as arresting as it is beguiling – a kind of architectural fever dream transplanted to a handsome Australian wilderness – but it is the images created by players that lodge deepest in the mind. Here’s one that has stuck with me: in the black of night, cicadas kicking up an almighty din, I had lost my partner. Panic. Despair. Fear. Then, there in the far distance, I saw him signalling in my direction. He was relentlessly spamming a gigantic, ball-shaped lamp on and off, the ground around him flicking from inky dark to warm pastel pink and back again, like a single Christmas light blinking from afar.
This kind of encounter is common in Big Walk, the brilliant and whimsical new online co-op puzzler from House House, the Melbourne-based studio behind the 2019 viral hit, Untitled Goose Game. Rather than playing as a honking, mischief-making goose as you do in that game, you are a bug-eyed, gangly limbed kind of bird person (think Pingu as drawn by Mondrian) for whom getting separated from your mates is all part of the fun. That’s somewhat because this rugged terrain is dense with vegetation and cliffs to fall down, and also because the game makes ingenious use of proximity and direction-based voice audio. Step out of earshot of your party and you will find it difficult to call for one another (unless, of course, you’ve picked up a Fisher-Price-like walkie-talkie).

There’s a ritual at the start of every event hosted by the Offline Project. Run by Pelé Zachariah, the activities vary – it could be a group walk, a collage‑making class or a supper club – but each one begins in the same way, *with an invitation to hand over your phone. Devices go in a lockbox. Once they’re all in, Zachariah closes the door and turns the key. “I don’t place them in for people, because it’s nice for them to physically put it in the box themselves, walk away, and think: for the next two or three hours, I’m fully present.”
He has been running these screen-free events in London since August 2025. First-timers can be apprehensive about being separated from their phone. “You can sense the vibe when they’re putting it away,” says Zachariah. “People have said to me, ‘I felt really weird’ or ‘I felt super uncomfortable for the first few minutes not having my phone on me.’ Then they’ll say, ‘I didn’t know how much I needed that.’”
